```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_gmmat <- requireNamespace("GMMAT", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("SeqVarTools", quietly = TRUE)
```

# Introduction

People with recent ancestry from more than one population, such as African
Americans, are called admixed. Along each of their chromosomes, some
segments were inherited from African ancestors and others from European
ancestors. Software such as RFMix can infer, for every segment and each of
the two copies of a chromosome, which population it came from. This is
called local ancestry.

Rare-variant association tests usually group the rare variants in a gene
and test whether carrying them is associated with a trait. If a variant's
effect depends on the genetic background it sits on, for example because
it is tagged by different nearby variants in African and European
haplotypes, pooling all carriers mixes carriers with and without the
effect, and the test loses power.

lantern uses local ancestry to split each person's count of alternate
alleles (their dosage, 0, 1 or 2) into one dosage per ancestry. A
heterozygote whose allele sits on an African haplotype contributes 1 to
the African dosage and 0 to the European dosage. lantern then runs the
gene-based SMMAT test from the GMMAT package separately for each ancestry,
and combines the per-ancestry p-values for each gene into one p-value with
the Cauchy combination test.

The analysis has three steps, one function each:

1. `ancestry_split()` reads a phased VCF and an RFMix local-ancestry file
   and returns one dosage matrix per ancestry.
2. `write_ancestry_gds()` saves each matrix as a `r Biocpkg("SeqArray")`
   GDS file, the format GMMAT reads.
3. `ancestry_smmat()` runs SMMAT on each GDS file and combines the
   results.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("lantern")
```

Step 3 also needs GMMAT (from CRAN) and SeqVarTools (from Bioconductor):

```{r install-suggests, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("GMMAT")
BiocManager::install("SeqVarTools")
```

```{r load}
library(lantern)
```

# Example data

lantern includes a small simulated dataset: 60 admixed individuals, 200
rare variants on chromosome 19 and eight genes. We simulated a continuous
trait `y` that is raised by alternate alleles in `GENE2`, but only when the
allele sits on an African haplotype. A good analysis should find `GENE2`
in the African-ancestry test and not in the European one.

```{r files}
ext <- system.file("extdata", package = "lantern")
vcf <- file.path(ext, "toy.vcf.gz")
msp <- file.path(ext, "toy.msp.tsv")
```

The VCF holds phased genotypes. A `|` separates the two copies of the
chromosome, so `0|1` means the alternate allele is on the second copy:

```{r vcf}
vcf_lines <- readLines(vcf)
data_lines <- vcf_lines[!startsWith(vcf_lines, "##")]
substr(data_lines[1:3], 1, 60)
```

The MSP file is RFMix's local-ancestry output. Its first line gives the
population codes (here 0 = AFR and 1 = EUR). Each later row is a segment
of the chromosome, with one ancestry call per sample and chromosome copy
(columns `S001.0`, `S001.1`, ...):

```{r msp}
substr(readLines(msp, n = 4), 1, 70)
```

# Step 1: split dosages by local ancestry

`ancestry_split()` matches samples between the two files, finds the
ancestry segment that contains each variant, and splits the dosages.

```{r split}
split <- ancestry_split(vcf, msp, mode = "dosage", chrom = "chr19",
                        verbose = FALSE)
```

The result has one variants x samples dosage matrix per population, named
after the populations in the MSP file:

```{r split-show}
split$AFR[1:4, 1:6]
split$EUR[1:4, 1:6]
```

Most entries are 0 because the variants are rare. `mode = "dosage"`
ignores phase. For a heterozygote with one African and one European
haplotype, the genotype alone does not say which haplotype carries the
allele, so the allele is shared between the two ancestries, with shares
estimated from the other carriers of the same variant. Here is the first
such heterozygote in the data; its two shares add up to its one allele:

```{r split-fraction}
i <- which(split$AFR %% 1 > 0, arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
c(AFR = split$AFR[i[1], i[2]], EUR = split$EUR[i[1], i[2]])
```

`vignette("split-intuition")` explains how the shares are calculated. With
phased data you can instead use `mode = "haplotype"`, which assigns every
allele to the ancestry of its own haplotype and never produces fractions.

The result also lists the variants that were kept. Variants with no
alternate allele in these samples are dropped
(`r split$overlap$n_monomorphic_filtered` here):

```{r kept}
head(split$variant_info)
split$overlap[c("n_common", "n_variants_kept", "n_monomorphic_filtered")]
```

# Step 2: write per-ancestry GDS files

GMMAT reads genotypes from GDS files, so each dosage matrix is saved to
its own file. The function returns the file paths, named by population.

```{r gds}
out_dir <- tempfile("lantern-")
gds <- write_ancestry_gds(split, out_dir, verbose = FALSE)
gds
```

# Step 3: test each gene in each ancestry

SMMAT needs three more inputs: a phenotype table, a kinship matrix and a
gene-group file. The phenotype table has one row per sample, with the
trait and covariates:

```{r pheno}
pheno <- read.delim(file.path(ext, "toy_pheno.tsv"))
head(pheno, 3)
```

The kinship matrix describes how related the samples are. Our simulated
samples are unrelated, so we use the identity matrix. In a real study this
would be a genetic relatedness matrix:

```{r kinship}
kinship <- diag(nrow(pheno))
dimnames(kinship) <- list(pheno$id, pheno$id)
```

The gene-group file assigns variants to genes. It has no header and six
columns: gene, chromosome, position, reference allele, alternate allele
and a weight. These are the 25 variants of `GENE2`:

```{r genes}
genes <- read.delim(file.path(ext, "toy_genes.tsv"), header = FALSE,
                    col.names = c("gene", "chr", "pos", "ref", "alt", "weight"))
head(genes[genes$gene == "GENE2", ])
table(genes$gene)
```

`ancestry_smmat()` fits the null model (the trait explained by the
covariates and relatedness, without genotypes) once, then runs SMMAT for
each ancestry. Passing `ancestry_counts` and `variant_info` from Step 1
weights the Cauchy combination by how many samples of each ancestry carry
a gene's variants, so the ancestry with more data counts for more.

```{r smmat, eval = has_gmmat}
res <- ancestry_smmat(gds, pheno, y ~ age + sex, kinship,
                      gene_group_file = file.path(ext, "toy_genes.tsv"),
                      ancestry_counts = split$ancestry_counts,
                      variant_info    = split$variant_info,
                      verbose = FALSE)
res$results
```

The table has one row per gene: `p_AFR` and `p_EUR` are the SMMAT p-values
from each ancestry, `w_AFR` and `w_EUR` the weights, and `p_cauchy` the
combined p-value. `GENE2` stands out:

```{r gene2, eval = has_gmmat}
res$results[res$results$gene == "GENE2", ]
```

Its African-ancestry p-value is very small, its European-ancestry p-value
is not, and the combined p-value keeps the signal. For comparison, we test
the same genes without splitting by ancestry. Adding the two dosage
matrices gives back each sample's total dosage:

```{r pooled, eval = has_gmmat}
pooled_gds <- file.path(out_dir, "pooled.gds")
write_dosage_gds(split$AFR + split$EUR, split$variant_info,
                 split$sample_ids, pooled_gds)
pooled <- ancestry_smmat(c(POOLED = pooled_gds), pheno, y ~ age + sex,
                         kinship, file.path(ext, "toy_genes.tsv"),
                         verbose = FALSE)
pooled$results[pooled$results$gene == "GENE2", c("gene", "p_POOLED")]
```

The pooled test also detects `GENE2`, with a p-value about three times
larger: carriers whose allele sits on a European haplotype add to the
pooled dosage without adding to the effect.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
```
